newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels reported closing in on Kisangani.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels reported closing in on Kisangani.

text.p: Defeated Zairean soldiers surrendered their weapons to rebels in the eastern town of Kindu on Wednesday and the rebel army was reported to be closing in on the strategic northeastern capital of Kisangani.
Kindu, up the rust red Zaire river from Kisangani, was captured by rebels on Sunday and a new administration installed.
Rebel officers said they collected arms from some of more than 80 former soldiers who gave up the fight and stayed behind when most of their comrades fled the town on Thursday.

A regional military source, who has closely monitored the war in Zaire since it started in October, said rebels were heading for Kisangani and had passed Bafwasende town, 230 km (140 miles) to the east.
He said the rebels were also 40 km (25 miles) beyond the town of Lubutu to the southeast heading for Kisangani, the army's main base in the east and Zaire's third largest city.
"There is no doubt that Kisangani is threatened and its fall could come in a very short period," the military source said.
The U.N. Department of Humanitarian Affairs quoted sources in Kinshasa saying Kisangani's governor flew to the capital on Wednesday. There was no independent confirmation of the report.
More than a dozen assault rifles and ammunition were stacked at the feet of rebels at a collection point in the centre of the KIndu, looted by the withdrawing soldiers and then its civilians.

"I cannot die for the money I was paid. When the attack started in Kindu I stayed at home. When my superiors told me to go and fight I refused," Myangezi Tshiabyera, a corporal wounded in fighting against the rebels last year, told reporters.

A corporal in Zaire's ragged and ill-disciplined army when he is paid receives a monthly salary of 120,000 New Zaires or less than a dollar. The exchange rate is 150,000 to the dollar in government-held territory and 90,000 in rebel-held areas.
Many among hundreds of teenagers and children who took to the streets waving branches and chanting slogans against ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko said they wanted to join the rebels.
Rebel officers held a public meeting in Kindu to name new local authorities to replace government officials who escaped before the fall of Kindu 400 km (250 miles) south of Kisangani.

The government on Tuesday ordered the expulsion of 40 U.N. relief workers who withdrew from Kisangani last weekend, saying their departure triggered a slaughter of Rwandan Hutus and displaced Zaireans.
A government statement said that 25,000 civilians had been slaughtered after rebels overran the Tingi Tingi refugee camp on Friday. There was no independent confirmation of such killings.
A total of 57 foreign aid workers left Kisangani by air last Saturday, saying increasing insecurity and harassment by local military authorities made it impossible for them to operate.
The U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) said on Wednesday people in the Great Lakes region faced famine because of civil war and refugee crises and urgent international action was needed.
"Pockets of famine could develop in eastern Zaire as relief distribution continues to be hampered by hostilities and logistic difficulties," FAO said in a report issued in Nairobi.

"Hundreds of thousands of Rwandan refugees and sections of the local population are inaccessible to relief agencies and are caught up in the middle of the fighting in the conflict zone. Deaths from malnutrition and disease are already reported."
In Brussels, the Belgian foreign ministry said Zaire had approved a five-point United Nations plan designed to end the war.
Guerrilla leader Laurent Kabila has said he is determined to end the 31-year rule of President Mobutu. He has spurned international pressure for a ceasefire.
